routes.title: Krom River (du Toit's to Waterfalls)

sections.Overview:
A linear in and out trail up the Krom River gorge to a series of spectacular pools and waterfalls. The walk to the first waterfall and pools is easy, after that there is some difficult exposed scrambling.
Key Statistics
sections.Route Description:
From the parking area the trail leads back towards the tunnel (as for the Elands River Trail). Look for a sign beneath the two bridges indicating the direction of the Krom River Trail. The trail crosses the Krom and Molenaars Rivers and leads for 2.5km (about 2.5 hours) to the Krom River waterfall. The first section (about 10 minutes) of the footpath follows the right bank of the Molenaars River in the direction of the old tunnel.
An alternative start (or finish) which is a little more "interesting" is start on the Elandspad path and at the bridge instead of going up Elandspad, cross the river on stepping stones.
When it reaches the Krom River the path follows the right side of the kloof. At the top end of the kloof the vegetation becomes more dense. The last section leads through indigenous riverine forest to the first waterfall.
There are two rock scrambles in order to go higher up the kloof to the top waterfall and huge pool. Definitely worth the extra effort, but scramble with care across a a sloping rock slab as it can be slippery. There are chains, so hold on tight!
These popular trails may be may be closed in winter after heavy rains when the river can be difficult and dangerous to cross.
But in any event, this is a trail best done in summer to enjoy the pools. Even then they are freezing, especially the big top pool.
Hikers are cautioned when climbing between the first and second waterfalls, and are advised to carry a rope. The second waterfall and large plunge pool are quite spectacular.
Krom River at du Toits

routes.title: Rockhopper Trail

sections: Rockhopper and Witte River from Bainskloof Pass road
sections.Location: Bainskloof
sections.Overview:
Linear trail from Eerste Tol to Tweed Tol down the Witte River
Key Statistics
sections.Route Description:
This linear trail in Bainskloof is moderate to difficult, depending on your level of fitness. The strenuous sections involve rock hopping, swimming and lots of adventure. Find your own way down the boulder-strewn riverbed surrounded by riverine bush.
Although most of the water obstacles can be side-stepped, there's no getting around a pool near Tweede Tol which you will have to wade through.  But for maximum fun, wat
erpro
of your pack
,
wear
kloofing shoes and simply walk or swim through every pool!
The trail starts at Eerste Tol in the Bainskloof Pass and follows the Witte River to the finish at the Tweede Tol picnic site. Because it is a linear trail, you will need a vehicle at the start and another at the finish.
The route is not open when the river is too high. Hazards include volatile weather, flooding rivers after rain, slippery rocks, wind and ticks!
Rockhopper 2
Chilling out en route - it can be very hot!

routes.title: Perdekop
routes.grade: 1 *** Just a walk, but with exquisite views

sections.Location:
Mont Rochelle Nature Reserve
(on top of the Franschhoek pass) up to the south-eastern tip of the Wemmershoek mountain range
Overview
: The cicular walk to Perdekop provides spectacular views of the Wemmershoek and Stettynskloof valleys, and of the surrounding mountain ranges. During winter months this is one of the easiest routes to get to snow.
sections.Route Description:
A day permit should be acquired (R40) at the Mont Rochelle nature reserve gate. After entering the gate, take the left hand path, marked Uitkyk. The Perdekop circular route is done by first walking to a Wemmershoek valley lookout point called Uitkyk. This route  is well marked. Follow the Uitkyk path in a northerly direction passing Breakfast rock (right) and the turnoffs to Du Toitskop (left).
The path stays on the left wall of a wide open valley. At the head of the valley (small nek) the path branches of to the right (easterly) - this is about 310 m before you reach the Uitkyk lookout point. It's highly recommended to continue on to the lookout point and backtrack to the turnoff.
From here the path is straightforward and well maintained. The route has a long slow incline and follows the a ridge adjacent to the Wemmershoek valley for about 3.2 km. After a few false peaks Perdekop can be seen as a prominent dome-ish peak. Here the path descends a bit into a marshy flat with a watercourse that runs down Perdekloof ravine. Cross the watercourse and follow the steepening path to the top of Perdekop. The Perdekop peak is marked with a large stone cairn, seen on the left in the panorama image above, and it has an elevation of 1575 m above sea level.
sections.Descent: The return path merges with the Perdekop path (from Uitkyk) just above the mentioned watercourse; be sure to keep left (coming down) at the split. Most of the path is a low to moderate decline; the last section of the path is a steep descent into the Dutoitsrivier gorge and a steep climb back up past the water pump station to the gate.
sections.Resources:
Mont Rochelle Nature Reserve Website
Map of Routes in Mont Rochelle
GPX Track of the route

A

routes.title: Wemmershoek Peak
routes.grade: 2*** * : Cross country hiking with occassional boulder hopping & rock steps. Exceptionally scenic

sections.Location:
Wemmershoek Peak (1766m), at the South-East extremity of the Wemmershoek Mountain range. Adjacent to Perdekop in the
Mont Rochelle Nature Reserve
, Franschhoek pass.
Overview
:
A spectactular & strenuous cross country hike (~22km with 1700m elevation gain), relatively accessible for such a large peak, a must do for any hikers. The peak is reached by crossing the large saddle seperating the peak from Perdekop. Note that the true summit of the Wemmershoek Mountains lies 1.5km North-West at 1793m on the large buttress above the Wemmershoek Peaklet, but this is unlabelled on most maps.

routes.title: Botmaskop
routes.grade: 3 *** Some scrambling lower down, milder scramble at top

sections.Location: Karindal Nature Reserve, Provinsie Road (near Rozendal), Stellenbosch
sections.Overview: Climb up to Bosmaskop and a traverse to the nek between Botmaskop and Square Tower peak (called Saaltjie), descending down to the Jonkershoek nature reserve gate.
sections.Route Description:
The full traverse is best planned with a group so as to place transport strategically. A group of six or more is also advised, as there have been several robberies on the lower approach slopes. Drop most of the party at the trail start which is at the small nature reserve in Provinsie Road (near Rozendal) Stellenbosch on the start of the Jonkershoek road. Drive all cars to Jonkershoek entrance car park. One car comes back to the start point and parks. Then we are ready to go. If you are intending just climb Bosmaskop, then start and finish is of course the same.
Cross the road and the grassy bank to reach the Bosmaskop reserve entrance Ignore the various side tracks – this one leads down to a gated dam - and follow the track up the hillside into a huge area of open burnt ground. The February 2017 fire raged across the hillsides, destroying large areas of pine and eucalyptus trees. Yes, non-indigenous trees, but the land seems poorer without them. Let’s hope that in time indigenous plants will again flourish and take over in this lunar landscape. The track now draws us inexorably upwards toward the battlements of Botmaskop as it towers out of the hillside above us.
The jeep track gives way to a bush trail that, pre-fire, was obvious and easy to follow, but now is tenuous at best, and is beset with gaunt burnt fallen stands of trees. The feint path traverses diagonally up until it is below the plug of rock rising above. Now the trail ascends to take on the challenge of Botmaskop itself. The fortification weak point is a gully that clefts the face from right to left, and our path leads up to this weakness. It seems improbable, but it goes without much fuss and a ‘few hands on’ rock moves. Continue up the gully and let it lead you on to the crux of the route.
Two views of the gully rock step. You may take this direct, or make a few moves left and move up on big holds to gain the gully continuation above.
Easier scrambling now leads up, past a ‘shoulder’ on the left, where you can regroup before taking on the final scramble to the top.
Rough scrambling to the left behind huge boulders takes you up towards the summit of Botmaskop.
Where you can walk above the clouds and take in the view to Simonsberg.
Decision time! Go back down, or carry on with the traverse of the ridge. Along the ridge not far from the summit is a short pavement of rock that leads to a narrow section of scramble that culminates in a downward scramble.
From here the ridge stretches on in a continuous line of minor summits. Some linked by a path showing through the resurgent undergrowth, but often showing no sign of a path what so ever! The general rule here is that though a traversing line round the hill seems inviting, the way along the summit ridges is the easiest, and does give glimpses of the pre-burn path. The exception to this is towards the later part of the ridge, where you should be able to pick out the original path leading left and across the escarpment, that leads on down and finally up to the edge of the ridge and the picnic table.
An obvious place to chill, take in the wonderful views and eat and drink the last of your vitals. The way down lies to your left as you descend the jeep track, down to the forest plantations. It is now that you enter the domain of the downhill mountain racers, and again, please look out for them. They are largely on ‘black’ bike trails, and have little room or time to manoeuvre round hikers.
There are many track variations here, but basically you are targeting a finish as close to the Jonkershoek reserve gate as possible. You are after minimising any walk along the tarmac road, at the end of a long tiring day.
Write-up courteously provided by
Steve Chadwick
.

routes.title: Diagonal Route on 3rd Ridge
routes.grade: 3 *** Lots of scrambling all the way, exposed

sections.Location:
From Witbrug (at the far end of circular road), up the Panorama path towards Bergrivier nek.
Overview
: One of the shortest routes to the top of a Jonkershoek Peak, following a clean line diagonally across the face of 3rd Ridge.
Route Description
:
(from Ernst Lotz,
Jonkershoek en sy Berge
) Numbers in [x] refer to corresponding slide.
Walk from the Witbrug parking [1] in the direction of Bergrivier nek, where the path meets the upper contour path. If you look up you will see slightly to the left a low pinnacle against the cliff [2]. Climb up to the small nek between the tower and the cliff. Then scramble up easy rock steps until a grass slope is reached. Walk up sloping to the right till a point is reached from where one looks down into a shallow ravine.
Follow the left hand edge of the ravine to the right under a prominent, concave overhang. Walk to the right over a broken grass slope that quickly changes to a broken ledge [3]. The ledge rises first and then narrows with slight exposure. Climb cautiously down at the end of the ledge, keeping as close to the cliff as possible - you actually move half under the cliff.
This brings you to easier terrain, where your route can vary a lot. The simplest is to scramble up to the right next to ledges and short rock steps to the prominent small nek a bit higher on (don’t try to climb up too quickly). The big platform to the right of the small nek is an ideal place to catch your breath and view the world [4]. Walk to the left around the pinnacle before you and scramble up in the corner. Shortly beyond the pinnacle the route meets the one that comes up from Bergrivier Nek [5] and the many cairns and slight path can easily be followed.
Follow an ascending traverse left around the south side of 3rd Ridge to a gully [10] and then up the final easy slope to the top [6] - there are many variations for this. (The line of cairns may lead you round to 2nd Ridge - keep more up than traverse.) The top has several summits - take your pick - they are all about the same height!
sections.Descent:
The quickest is back the same way. The easiest is
via Bergrivier Nek.
Alternatively,  over 2nd Ridge and down Slab Route, but only if you have been up it before or have a GPS. The top of Slab Route can be difficult to find, and almost impossible in mist. See [11] to [23] for this route.
MM 3rd Ridge via Diagonal Route Rev 2

routes.title: Klipspringer

sections:
Looking up at ridge from start
Looking onto ridge from Swartboskloof.  Route follows skyline as much as possible.
sections.Location: Jonkershoek, off Swartboskloof
sections.Overview: A pleasant and interesting alternative to the usual up and down Swartboskloof.   Has some interesting and varied scrambling.
sections.Route Description:
Start at the Swartboskloof parking and proceed up Swartboskloof to 850m.  See map for turn off point.
There are two alternative starts. the first is just before the path goes through the gully and the other is just after.  The first is more "pure" (and difficult) but the latter is fine and more obvious.  Take the first if you see it, the second if you miss it!
The route goes up the ridge more or less through a series of rockbands.  Keep to the ridge as much as possible, but there are easier options off the right.
At the top of the ridge descend to the Klipspringer Vlakte. Stop for a swim in one of the many delightful pools (if you can withstand the chill!), then walk upstream to reach the Panorama path.
Return via Swartboskloof.
A fun diversion is to scramble up Pic Sans Nom view point or peak (
see map
) for stunning views over the Hottentots Holland.
Klipspringer

routes.title: Panorama Route

sections.Location: Jonkershoek Nature Reserve, Stellenbosch
sections.Overview:
This is Jonkershoek's premier official route, it includes breathtaking views of Assegaaiboskloof,  the Cape Peninsula, False Bay, the Hottentots Holland mountain range, and, of course, the beautiful Jonkershoek ridges. The route starts up the Northern side of the valley and circles to the Southern side, coming down Swartboskloof.
There is a shorter variation, which comes down Kurktrekker (the path leading up to First and Second Waterfall); or one can start up Kurtrekker, circle right and down Swartboskloof; or circle left and down at Berg River Nek i.e many possibilities!

routes.title: Sentralekloof

sections.Location: The route starts on the Contour Path in the Sentralekloof watercourse (between Square Tower Peak and Twins).
sections.Overview: A long route that starts in Sentralekloof and makes use of an extremely long "B" graded gully to reach Twin Peaks.
sections.Route Description:
To reach the route you will have to find you way to the Contour Path between
Square Tower Peak and Twins
. The route starts in the Sentralekloof watercourse. The Nerinakloof and Sentralekloof watercourses are very close to each other, be sure to take the right-hand one.
Ascend Sentralekloof until it looks like the ravine reaches a dead end. Traverse out to the right onto the obvious grass slope. The start of this traverse is well cairned, so look out for a set of cairns close together. Continue to traverse all around to the front of the mountain.
Here you should enter an extremely long, and steep rocky gully. Some sections of the gully require B / B+ grade scrambling. At some point the gully forces you to the right. If you look out there should be an easy traverse out of the gully and onto a rocky section, which is easy scrambling to a neck at the top of the gully.
From the neck you should head in the direction of the upper part of Sentralekloof, first decending and then doing multiple descends and ascends of short grassy sections. During these sections you need to stay close to the rock face but do NOT attempt climb up the narrow gully on your right! After a short scramble you should enter the upper section of Sentralekloof, which is ascended to the neck between the Twin Peaks. From here the path the either peak is obvious.
sections.Descend: The most obvious ascend is down Langrivierkloof. You can also follow the watershed in the direction of Botmaskop and descend via the Nerinakloof route.  This route makes use of a short upper section of Vensterkloof, a rocky gully known as "Bakoond", Nerinakloof, and a steep gully left of Nerinakloof known as "Sit-Sit".

stats.Time: 4-6 hrs up, 3-5 down depending on route

sections.Location:
Connects the Jonkershoek contour path to the col between 1st Ridge & 2nd Ridge Peaks near to the Kloktoring.
- The route is marked. Follow the Jonkershoek watershed for descent routes.
Overview
:
A relatively easy ascent to the col near the Kloktoring between 1st Ridge (Rifberg) & 2nd / 3rd ridge peaks (Katedraal) but which must rank as one of the steepest hiking routes in the Cape. Only rated *** directly from Ernst Lotz's book and due Jonkershoek's high standards, but a fantastic route well worth doing. Often used as a descent route after more technical ascents.
It couples with visits to either 1st Ridge or one or more of 2nd & 3rd Ridge & the South-Eastern Groot Drakenstein peaks (Banghoek, Isolation, Easter & Bulkop). Langrivierkloof is a more enjoyable option to reach 1st Ridge.
Route Description
:
This route description can be suplemmented by Ernst Lotz's description in
Jonkershoek en sy Berge
- an english translation can be found on the main Jonkershoek page. This is catered towards the ascent of 2nd Ridge Peak.
Begin at the Jonkershoek reserve main gate, and head immediately up to the contour path - there is a maize of paths to reach it but make sure not to take mountain bike paths. Follow the contour path, at the South-East corner of the twin peaks - just before Langrivierkloof - the path will transition from jeeptrack to foot path. Keep following this past the Virgin & 1st Ridge Peaks until the Prominent pinnacles between 1st & 2nd Ridge become clear (Slide 4). You will pass the Jakkalsvlei watercourse,  and then very soon another unnamed watercourse, follow the path another ~200m until just beyond a curve around a small ridge. This should land you beneath an orange coloured cliff face, the left most of the large pinnacles. Turn off the contour path and ascend the grassy slope, after a short period a vague path will become apparent.
You will soon reach a tree rest spot right beneath this orange cliff, at approximately the same height head left and traverse the top of the grassy band beneath the tall rock bands. At the far corner, turn right and choose any number of B grade scrambles up the rock band which will soon lead you to wider grassy ledges. Navigate a few more scrambles until you reach the main ravine, this is extremely steep but not technical. Follow this all the way to the top of the col between 1st and 2nd Ridge Peaks. To head to 1st Ridge Peak, follow the knife edge left - this involves some exposed ledges. To head to 2nd Ridge Peak, turn right and follow a grassy recess to the peak which is quite close by.
sections.Descent:
Slab route itself is a popular descent route. The bergriviernek knife edge connecting 3rd Ridge Peak to the Panorama trail is the most common descent route from 2nd Ridge. Class 2 (A+/B) but very exposed in places and with some tricky navigation in places. A more detailed guide can be found
here
.
Langrivierkloof is the most common descent from 1st Ridge Peak, requires traversing narrow ledges around the Virgin Peaks although the actual kloof is quite straightforward.
MM Jonkershoek Slab Route
Thank you to David Williams for providing most of the high quality photos used in the slides.

stats.Grade: 3 *** : Short class 3 section with significant class 2 sections to reach final peak(s)
stats.Height Gain: 1400m: Jonkershoek reserve gate (240m) to 1st Ridge (1515m) or 2nd Ridge peaks (1517m) + contour path undulation. ~100m extra to 3rd Ridge
stats.Time: 10 Hours: 5h ascent to Col + 1h to 1st/2nd Ridge. 4 Hours descent via Langrivierkloof or Bergriviernek

routes.title: Swartboskam

sections.Location:
Jonkershoek, starting at the parking for Swartboskloof.
Overview
: A long exposed ridge parallel to Swartboskloof. Cross country all the way, but the ridge is mainly clear of bush.
sections.Route Description:
Follow the Swartboskloof path for about 300m. Where it passes close to the weir, cross over and climb a steep busy bank to gain the ridge. Not pleasant, but not long and once on the ridge the going is a lot easier. Alternatively, take off directly onto the ridge from the road - it may be less bushy.
Follow the line of the ridge all the way up, moving to the right of the first rock step. Higher, one traverses with a rock wall on one's right. At the end of that go up right to small nek and then an ascending traverse around to the left to regain the ridge. Continue to the top of the ridge.
At the top of the ridge drop down onto the Klipspringer Vlakte with many amazing pinnacles, rock formations and lovely pools. Continue 2km up this valley finding the easiest way on either left or right to minimize bush to finally meat the Panorama path near Pic Sans Nom.
Return via Swartboskloof.
Swartboskam

stats.Height gain: 800m: from 360m at road to 1160m at Panorama path
stats.Time: 6-7 hrs up, 3 down

routes.grade: 1/2 ***: A few steep sections with optional ladders/fixed ropes. Overwhelmingly good class 1 path

sections.Location:
Bloupunt Peak above Montague, accessed by following Donkerkloof. Donkerkloof can be accessed several ways, this description begins from the Cogmanskloof Link Trail on
Waboomsdraai Road
. It can also be started from the Cogmanskloof contour path or
Montague Mountain Reserve Gate
(R83 Permit).
sections.Overview: The path meanders across the streams running through the beautiful jungle like Donkerkloof, and then up the ridges to the peak. The peak offers near panoramic views of the area, and features a dial labelling the towns visible below (Including Montagu, Ashton, Robertson, Bonnievale, and others.). Once above the forest there is little shade so its best to overpack on water, whether the kloof water is safe to drink is doubtful.
sections.Route Description: The path is well maintained and marked and therefore no explicit description is necessary, the image captions are there to supplement the experience. The Donkerkloof section of the path is out & back, but a large section of the path is circular and can therefore be done in either direction. Clockwise (The way implied by signage) is steeper but offers morning shade as it is on the South Face. Anti-Clockwise has more gentle gradients and is generally more scenic - including three short detours to waterfalls - the photos are displayed for the anti-clockwise route.

routes.title: Anysberg

sections:
Anysberg offers 4x4 drives, horse riding and mountain biking (mainly along the 4x4 roads), and kayaking on the Rooi Damme.
Accommodation is in self catering cottages (only Agama has it's own ablutions, the others share). A magnificent campsite has at present got no toilets or shower facility.
There are 3 hikes possible, though none are on dedicated trails.
The walk to Land se Kloof is on an eroded old farm track into the kloof, then a rough trail enters the kloof some way. Best spot to picnic is at the old weir, as after that the path is bushier, and higher up the kloof involves boulder hopping.
The longest hike is to Tapfontein, and it involves an 8km drive to the turnoff, then the 4x4 road is walked there and back. This is more pleasant than it sounds, though after rains you have to find a way to cross the river soon after leaving the main road. On the way to Tapfontein is a short detour to some unremarkable bushman paintings. (Very fit hikers may decide to walk the entire 4x4 route from Vrede, though the return via the main road would be a real trudge!)
The hike into Prinspoort involves driving 15km from the cottages or campsite almost all the way to the Main entrance. The obvious thing would be to try to get permission to do it on your way in if you enter from the Ladismith side, but most people would not want to park with all their stuff left in the vehicle.
For more information on the Reserve, and how to get there, see the Cape Nature website page at:
http://www.capenature.org.za/reserves.htm?reserve=Anysberg+Nature+Reserve&PHPSESSID=0632b580d841b40afc8ad56e27e48b4b#reserve_tabs

routes.grade: 1 **** 14km on fairly good path

sections.Location: Ladismith, off the road to Hoekoe, Western Cape,
sections.Overview: The approx. 14 km trail path has been recently cleared (Sept 2010) and although in good condition, still needs care on the steep rocky sections.
sections.Route Description:
A pleasant trail, with an interesting background as it resulted from Stanley de Witt's idea of placing a light visible from Ladismith, which was powered by a waterwheel generating the electricity from a perennial stream high up on Elandsberg (also called Toringberg).

routes.title: Dwarsrivier Lot's Wife Trail

sections:
This delightful trail on the Nieuwoudt family's Dwarsrivier farm is a marvellous introduction to the fantastic and beautiful Cederberg rock formations that make this mountain region so special.
The trail is fairly short (3,58 km approx), is reasonably flat so not strenuous, but you can spend a morning or afternoon just enjoying the views and the amazing pillars, arches, and gargoyles.
Please enquire at the Office at Dwarsrivier farm for access permission.
NB this Google Earth image is NOT A GPS track but has been drawn in. However no great navigational or Hiking skill is needed to follow this well set out trail path.
Cederberg Lot's Wife Trail

routes.title: Kromriver farm Disa pool hike
routes.grade: 1 *** path overgrown in several places

sections.Overview: The most popular day walk from Kromriver farm.
sections.Route Description:
Arrange permission for this hike from the Nieuwoudts at Kromriver farm. As Disa pool is on land owned by the Andrag family, there is a conservation fee payable.
Walking from the farm adds an hour extra each way so better to drive (carefully) along the rough road and park opposite the Skilderkliphuis cave just before the track descends to the river. Follow the last bit of eroded track to the river, where the path splits and one can either cross, or continue. Both ways lead to the Oak Tree (Now totally burnt and may eventually disappear).
Here one chooses to either follow the river trail to the pool and back, or a short way beyond the Oak, take a bushy diagonal gully up to the shaleband path and follow that until it descends to Disa pool. On the map you can see that the shaleband path can also be started at a turnoff some distance before the end of the road.
Kromriver cave may be visited along the way from either route, but unless you have been shown how to descend from the shaleband, it is easier from the river path.
MM Cederberg Krom River Disa Pool

routes.title: Kromriver Farm Rensie's TV Mast hike

sections:
This pleasant easy hike of just over 5 km takes one along the Kromriver ridge with lovely views into the valleys on both sides.
Starting up the path to the MCSA Breekkrants property, which is marked by a sign saying 'TV Kop'. At the MCSA sign on the nek, scramble up onto the ridge.  Follow beacons (stone cairns) and at a fence in a dip carefully go through the wires (not barbed) and continue up and along the ridge.
The vague track descends to the TV Mast access road where a short distance to the right (South) the beaconed path leads up to the Mast.   After enjoying the view, return to the road and follow it down all the way past the Pump Storage dam construction to join the Truitjieskraal road.  Turn left and back to the Farm.
In 2021 Derik Nieuwoudt arranged a new section of path that starts some way below the nek and traverses across to the old road to the mast. Lower down the road the new path branches off to contour across the vlakte and eventually to re-join the road.
The
kmz track file is available for download

routes.description:
This pleasant easy hike of just over 5 km takes one along the Kromriver ridge with lovely views into the valleys on both sides.
Starting up the path to the MCSA Breekkrants property, which is marked by a sign saying 'TV Kop'. At the MCSA sign on the nek, scramble up onto the ridge.  Follow beacons (stone cairns) and at a fence in a dip carefully go through the wires (not barbed) and continue up and along the ridge.
The vague track descends to the TV Mast access road where a short distance to the right (South) the beaconed path leads up to the Mast.   After enjoying the view, return to the road and follow it down all the way past the Pump Storage dam construction to join the Truitjieskraal road.  Turn left and back to the Farm.
In 2021 Derik Nieuwoudt arranged a new section of path that starts some way below the nek and traverses across to the old road to the mast. Lower down the road the new path branches off to contour across the vlakte and eventually to re-join the road.

routes.title: Maltese Cross hike
routes.grade: 1 **** Good clear easy path

sections.Location: Cederberg southern, starting from Dwarsrivier farm.
sections.Overview: One of the 'must see' rock formations in the Cederberg
sections.Route Description:
The Nieuwoudt's at Dwarsrivier farm are able to issue you with a permit (free to Wild Card holders, otherwise pay the day hike charge). This allows you to traverse the Cape Nature part of the Cederberg Reserve on the path to the Maltese Cross.
The rough access road of several Km is on Dwarsrivier property, and starts from the turnoff to the Cederberg Observatory. There is a locked gate, but the combination to the lock will be provided on your permit.  Cape Nature's boundary is some way beyond the Parking area, at a sign saying somewhat misleadingly: "Bokveldskloof".

routes.title: Cederberg Rooiberg Trail
routes.grade: 2 ** (could be 3* if descent and river path sections improved)

sections.Location: Southern Cederberkg/Karoo, from the Esterhuizen's Nuwerust Farm Restcamp on the Matjiesrivier/Ceres road.
sections.Overview:
This 12km, 5-6hr hike starts at the Esterhuizen's Nuwerust Restcamp, and takes a scrambling line under the impressive Rooiberg cliffs where rock climbers can enjoy some free and some bolted  climbs. The path continues steeply up around the far corner to climb above the cliff,  then crosses the easy but lengthy plateau and descends via a rocky ridge into a gully and slope which should be treated with care. On reaching the Brandkraal river sandy cattle tracks are followed on the North bank past cave formations and through some unfortunate invasive alien vegetation to return to the farm.
MM Nuwerust Rooiberg Trail

routes.title: Tafelberg Gully Route
routes.grade: B

sections:
MM Cederberg Tafelberg Gully Route
The Cederberg Tafelberg is the second highest peak in the range with 2 summit beacons at 1964 and 1968m respectively. NB this is a difficult peak to climb and the Gully route at grade 'B' is the easiest way up. The final section of the route involves an exposed and awkward step over a gap onto the smooth waterchute at the head of which the chain can be used to get up the strenuous and slippery vertical finish. The descent is even more tricky and this route is best done with an experienced leader.
Access is usually from the Welbedacht parking area off the road to Driehoek Farm, and as it is in the Cape Nature Reserve a permit should be obtained (often easiest at the Algeria offices as they can advise on current conditions).
A day trip is strenuous so most parties will want to overnight in one of the caves at Welbedacht, Spout, or Panorama.
NB Water is often a problem and either carry sufficient or be sure to know how and where to find it. Hygienic Toilet practice must be observed as especially Welbedacht cave is overused and the water supply must not be compromised so walk around to use the area behind and above the cave.
If the slideshow does not work automatically click on the 3 vertical dots and from the drop down window click 'Auto play' and from the options select '5 seconds' and 'loop' then click 'Play' at the top of the window. If the slideshow is working and you want to stop to go back to look at something, such as read the page of description, then use the arrowheads either side of the slide number.
A good map is recommended such as Slingsby's one of the Southern Cederberg.

routes.title: Truitjieskraal trail
routes.grade: 1 **** easy path

sections.Location: Matjiesrivier Nature Reserve, Southern Cederberg
sections.Overview: A short but fascinating hike through fantastic Cederberg rock scenery in the Matjiesrivier reserve. (Permit required which is obtainable from Kromriver Farm or Matjiesrivier office. No charge to Wild Cardholders)
sections.Route Description:
See captions on slideshow.
The turnoff to Truitjieskraal from the Matjiesrivier to Kromriver dirt road, is at a
Cape Nature sign (see picture) where there is  a chain with a combination lock. You get given the combination with your permit.
Drive to the first parking area where the trail starts. The second and third parking areas are for quick access to the Bushman paintings. The end of the trail takes you down to the middle parking area, and there is then a short walk back on the road to the car.

routes.title: Wolfberg Cracks

sections:
The Wolfberg Cracks is one of the best known and spectacular parts of the magnificent Cederberg. The Cracks are on private land adjacent to the Wilderness area, and a permit must be obtained from the Nieuwoudts at Dwarsriver farm.
The Arches route up the Cracks requires some rock scrambling fitness and agility, and many parties are content to just go up and down the easier Descent Crack (aka Adderley Street or Gaper Crack).
In recent times the Dwarsrivier management has added some signposts and equipped the difficult Arches Cracks with bolted handholds and a safety rope/cable in appropriate places.
Camping and cottage accommodation at Sandrift, near the start of the way up to the Cracks, is also available by arrangement with the Nieuwoudts.
Wolfberg Cracks Photo Guide for Mountain Meanders

routes.title: Otter Trail
routes.grade: 1 **** Superb experience

sections.Location: Tsitsikamma National Park accessed from the N2 Highway through the Garden Route
sections.Overview:
One of the early National Hiking Trails and possibly the most famous for the splendid coastal scenery and the challenges of the many river crossings.
The potential seriousness of Bloukrans river crossing should not be underestimated and be sure to obtain full information in advance.
The trail is best enjoyed taking the full 4 nights and 5 days, though it has been run in a day !
There are escape routes at each hut, which are sometimes used if the next river crossing is dangerously in flood.
Use the SAN Parks website for maps to download and Park and Trail fees and to do a booking.
https://www.sanparks.org/parks/garden_route/camps/storms_river/tourism/otter.php
MM Otter Trail 5 Day version

routes.title: Robberg Trail

sections.Location: Plettenberg Bay off the N2
sections.Overview:
As easy trail with spectacular views (including many seals) and varied geology and vegetation. A plus is the trail passes cave sites of archeological and anthropological interest.
Note
: Permits obtainable from Cape Nature or at the office entrance to the Reserve.
sections.Route Description:
The trail is well signposted and on a clear path with sections of boardwalk and protection railings or chains where needed.
The hiking is moderate with only a few steep sections and a short section of beach walking. If the full circuit is done it takes at least 4 hours and is advisable to allow for Morning Tea and Lunch stops along the way.
MM Robberg Trail

routes.title: Duiwelskloof

sections:
Location
:
Languedoc, Franschhoek, Valley
Overview
: A long, difficult route with extensive scrambling up a narrow kloof.
All Trails
has a two alternative trails in and around Duiwelskloof.
sections.Route Description:
Access and parking arrangements have changed from time to time. Enquire locally.
From the parking at Languedoc, proceed up a well marked path to the entrance of the kloof, which at this point looks like a solid rock wall. Enjoy this short section of path - it's the last until the top!  Careful careful note of the way as you may be descending in the dusk which happens unexpected early in this deep shady kloof.
Boulder hop on rough terrain up the kloof bearing left towards Devil's Tooth, the pinnacle to the left of Hutchinson Peak (see map).  Do not go up to the nek between Devil's Tooth and Hutchinson. Continue scrambling up bearing right to the base of a long sloping rock wall on the left hand side.
Climb this wall on exposed rock with minimal handholds - but it slopes back at an easy angle. Be careful of any loose rock. Exit into the narrow kloof and follow this to the top which brings out on top of the Drakenstein.
Drakenstein Peak, Eikenhof Peak, Dragoon Buttress and Dragoon Peak are within reach (see map) but 100 to 200m higher so add a lot on. Make sure you allow enough time as the descent is the same way and takes almost as long with the continuous boulder hopping taking a toll at the end of a long day.
MM Duiwelskloof

routes.title: Boskloof Ridge
routes.grade: 3 *** (B-route) and 5 **** (C-route)

sections.Location:
On the south side of Steenbras Gorge, 6km south of Gordon's Bay. (See also
Steenbras Ridge
on the north side.)  For access notes see
Crystal Pools
sections.Overview: A spectacular ridge route with two alternative finishes - an easy B route and challenging C-route. The entire route is cross country except for the return down past Crystal Pools.
sections.Route Description:
Two new scrambling routes have been opened on this spectacular ridge overlooking the Steenbras Gorge.   The B route follows a clean rocky ridge with several knife edges overlooking False Bay (like Woody Buttress but more fun).
The route starts just 20m after the gate on the path leading up to Crystal Pools.  Go up to the ridge and follow the ridge all the way, keeping as much to the edge as possible. There are 4 rock steps on the way which are climbed either straight up or to the right. At the top where the ridge ends at a 100m high rock band, traverse left on easy ground and up to a prominent cave.
The B-route branches off left from just below the cave over a small nek and down a long, steep slab into a ravine.  This ravine is followed to the top. The descent is down an easy, broken slope into the top of Steenbras and the down through Crystal Pools.
From the cave, the 'C route' goes right up a steep rock slab.  When this runs out, ascend a 5m pitch to the next level and then traverse right around the corner, and then keep traversing across the face of Boskloof Peak.
"Carrell's Ledge on steroids" was an apt description as it is about three times as long and much more exposed than Carrell's.  Definitely needs a very good head for heights - the exposure is severe and the ledges tiny.
About 500m along the traverse the ledge runs out.  Do a 20m abseil (or an awkward C downclimb) to the lower ledge to continue the traverse. (The best abseil point is a large block - needs about 5m of ab cord.)
The continuation of the traverse on the lower ledge includes a scary 50m across a rather thin, sandy section until the ledge widens. This traverse exits on the ridge from where one can reach the top by an easy pleasant ascending diagonal scramble through broken ground. The descent is down an easy, but very long, slope to the top of Steenbras and then down through Crystal Pools.
The route does have some dangers as the long traverses cannot be protected and participants need to be confident of moving unroped on exposed terrain.  Care also needs to be exercised on the abseil to avoid the rope, or abseilers, dislodging rocks on those below as there is a lack of space at the bottom, especially for a larger party.  The first person down should do a vigorous cleaning and it would be better for the party to continue along the traverse after each person has abseiled and not wait for the rest of the party.
sections.C-route: First explored by Tony Heher, Martyn Trainor, Lucille Krige, Jeanne Myburgh and Dennis Lange on an MCSA meet on 21 May 2009 and completed by Tony Heher, Karen Watkins, Kenny Hoffman and Siggie Sixt on 16 May 2010 as part of a Meridian meet.
sections.B-route:
Tony Heher, Margie Growse, Martin Trainor, Lucille Krige, Jeanne Myburgh, Peggy de Kock and Kathy Holthausen - U3A meets in June & August 2008.
The route opening story makes an interesting tale:
A lazy meet to
Crystal Pools
on a hot summer day in March 2008 led to some idle speculation as to possible routes on the ridges to the north and south of the Steenbras Gorge.  Later inquiries indicated that neither was known as a route made us even more interested.
Returning in June 2008, the north ridge was climbed and nicknamed the Dinosaurus-kam after the rugged 5-humped ridge between Gordons Bay and Steenbras. An interesting "find" on this exploration was an occupied hide-out near the top of Steenbras Peak. This route is an easy B. See
Steenbras Ridge
for a description.
In August the south ridge up Boskloof Peak was climbed. This proved to be a beautiful clean line on rock most of the way with a series of dramatic knife edges overlooking the coast running down towards Hangklip. One of these really classy classic routes!
Where the ridge ended against the upper cliffs of Boskloof Peak, things got interesting.  A steep, exposed ramp up and around the corner looked C-interesting, but with time short, we took an easier B-exit down a series of steep slabs into the ravine and an easy line to the top. The descent was via Crystal Pools where we had a well deserved swim, despite the winter afternoon, after 9 hours of rough cross country going.
Intrigued by the possibilities of the C-ramp, Tony, Lucille and Jeanne returned early in September for another look, got a bit further but still did not complete the traverse.  The home trip this time was made "interesting" by the Steenbras being in flood. The raging waterfalls were wonderful, the two swims across the freezing flooded river at 5pm on a chilly winter afternoon, a little less so!
Undeterred we returned in May 2009 for another try.  This nearly aborted before we even got out of the cars because of the fearsome lightening storm that was raging as we drove out.   This time we made it nearly all the way across the traverse before turning back.  Several further attempts to finish the route never got off the ground (for some strange reason I seemed to be running out of willing victims... err, I mean climbing partners) until I persuaded Meridian to give it a go. So it was only on the 4th attempt that it was finally completed.
With thanks to all my companions who have stoically put up with being dragged through lightning storms, the bush backward (and every other way) and half naked through freezing flood waters all in pursuit of that holy grail, a classic new route.
Tony Heher
Boskloof Ridge
MCSA meet on 9 April 2011:
Miles Adams, Laura De Rose, Brian de Villiers, Ed February, Tony Heher (Convenor), Charmaine Kritzinger, Vanessa Muhl, Jeanne Myburgh (Co-convenor), Anne Price, Paul Verhoeven and Ezan Wilson
Some comments from
participants
:
Thanks for an absolutely wonderful day in the mountains! This was not your average hike/scramble/climb. I have some adjectives to describe it: cross-country, ridge scrambling, bushwacking, abseiling, adventurous, nail biting, nerve-wracking, exposed traversing, exciting, adrenaline rushing, skinny dipping, .....Thanks Tony, Ed, and Jeanne for guiding us safely. I'm sure all of us would like to see more of this type of mountaineering, all packaged into a single outing. It was absolutely awesome. What else can I say ?!!
Carrell's Ledge on steroids? You must be kidding! Carrell's is positively sedate... this was more like Carrell's on LSD... what a trip.
I thoroughly enjoyed the route... It was just the kind of scrambling and exploration that appeals to me, especially as I've always had a particular fondness for traverses, so I found it very satisfying. But I wouldn't expect everyone to share my view, and participants should read up in advance and get a good idea of what to expect.
I can understand that some would have liked some protection on the traverse, but I can't honestly see where and how one would provide it. To my mind it was the kind of traversing which is best done with care and concentration, rather than complicated ropes. Although the ledges weren't always generous they were adequate.
Closing Steenbras for a year or more seemed a heavy handed approach .... Having seen the damage first hand it's understandable why this is necessary. The badly eroded top sections need a massive amount of rehabilitation. Look forward to revisiting this stunning valley when it is open again.

Where the ridge ended against the upper cliffs of Boskloof Peak, things got interesting.  A steep, exposed ramp up and around the corner looked C-interesting, but with time short, we took an easier B-exit down a series of steep slabs into the ravine and an easy line to the top. The descent was via Crystal Pools where we had a well deserved swim, despite the winter afternoon, after 9 hours of rough cross country going.
Intrigued by the possibilities of the C-ramp, Tony, Lucille and Jeanne returned early in September for another look, got a bit further but still did not complete the traverse.  The home trip this time was made "interesting" by the Steenbras being in flood. The raging waterfalls were wonderful, the two swims across the freezing flooded river at 5pm on a chilly winter afternoon, a little less so!
Undeterred we returned in May 2009 for another try.  This nearly aborted before we even got out of the cars because of the fearsome lightening storm that was raging as we drove out.   This time we made it nearly all the way across the traverse before turning back.  Several further attempts to finish the route never got off the ground (for some strange reason I seemed to be running out of willing victims... err, I mean climbing partners) until I persuaded Meridian to give it a go. So it was only on the 4th attempt that it was finally completed.
With thanks to all my companions who have stoically put up with being dragged through lightning storms, the bush backward (and every other way) and half naked through freezing flood waters all in pursuit of that holy grail, a classic new route.
Tony Heher
Boskloof Ridge
MCSA meet on 9 April 2011:
Miles Adams, Laura De Rose, Brian de Villiers, Ed February, Tony Heher (Convenor), Charmaine Kritzinger, Vanessa Muhl, Jeanne Myburgh (Co-convenor), Anne Price, Paul Verhoeven and Ezan Wilson
Some comments from
participants
:
Thanks for an absolutely wonderful day in the mountains! This was not your average hike/scramble/climb. I have some adjectives to describe it: cross-country, ridge scrambling, bushwacking, abseiling, adventurous, nail biting, nerve-wracking, exposed traversing, exciting, adrenaline rushing, skinny dipping, .....Thanks Tony, Ed, and Jeanne for guiding us safely. I'm sure all of us would like to see more of this type of mountaineering, all packaged into a single outing. It was absolutely awesome. What else can I say ?!!
Carrell's Ledge on steroids? You must be kidding! Carrell's is positively sedate... this was more like Carrell's on LSD... what a trip.
I thoroughly enjoyed the route... It was just the kind of scrambling and exploration that appeals to me, especially as I've always had a particular fondness for traverses, so I found it very satisfying. But I wouldn't expect everyone to share my view, and participants should read up in advance and get a good idea of what to expect.
I can understand that some would have liked some protection on the traverse, but I can't honestly see where and how one would provide it. To my mind it was the kind of traversing which is best done with care and concentration, rather than complicated ropes. Although the ledges weren't always generous they were adequate.
Closing Steenbras for a year or more seemed a heavy handed approach .... Having seen the damage first hand it's understandable why this is necessary. The badly eroded top sections need a massive amount of rehabilitation. Look forward to revisiting this stunning valley when it is open again.

routes.title: Crystal Pools at Steenbras
routes.grade: 1 *** or 2 if one goes up to the top pools

sections.Location:
6km south of Gordon's Bay on the R44.   (See also
Steenbras Ridge
and
Boskloof Ridge
- two adventurous climbs on either side of the gorge.
)
sections.Overview:
A gorge with a magnificent set of pools. Ideal for a lazy summer day!
NB
.  For a year from 1 May 2011 the area was closed for rehabilitation.
Access
: This is a City Council controlled area and permits (R60 pp) must be obtained in advance by emailing
steenbras.naturereserve@capetown.gov.za
Crystal Pools is very popular on summer weekends and numbers are limited. Advance booking is essential. The area is closed in winter (1 May to 31 Oct)
sections.Route Description:
From the parking on the R44 (100m south of the bridge) it is an easy walk up the gorge, crossing the river three times before the bottom pool is reached in about an hour.
From there, take you pick (or find a free pool!) and explore up to the next 3 pools. The path does get steeper and there is some easy scrambling involved.
If you have the time, it is worth continuing up the gorge on the left (Grade 2) to the top pool, with breathtaking views of all the pools and waterfalls as one goes.
MM Steenbras Gorge

routes.title: Hangklip  @ Pringle Bay

sections.Location: Pringle Bay, Overberg
sections.Overview:
A fun walk up a valley at the back of Hangklip to stunning 360 degree views over False Bay and the Overberg coast
Key Statistics
sections.Route Description:
Start in Clarence Drive in Pringle Bay. Follow the clear path up the valley. At a junction, take the right hand path up to the Summit.
Enjoy the views 33 km to the west across False Bay to Cape Point , 61 km to Table Mountain, 36 km to the East to Hermanus and 52 km to Gansbaai.  And below your feet is the Hangklip lighthouse.
Fastest and simplest return is back via the same path but there are a number of more interesting alternatives: (see the OSM map)
Go down the faint path on the ridge facing False Bay. Take the path off to the right down a busy gully to High Level Road and follow the round around back to Pringle, using the shortcut track over the nek between Hangklip and Pringle Bay Peak.
Continue down the ridge to meet the path coming up the valley. Turn left and proceed back to the parking.
Or turn right and go down to the path past the Bleskop sandboarding dunes and and return via
Brodie Link
. Or, if cars are at both ends,  cross Silversands Beach to your cars at Baumgartner Place in Betty's Bay.
Note
: Seafarm is a private nature reserve with restricted access. Inquire locally or obtain a permit before entering.
Hangklip from High Level  road.  The path from Pringle runs up behind the ridge visible here.
There is also a rock climbing route up the right hand ridge and an an interesting scramble via the gully in the center of the picture, but this crosses private land so access permission is required.

routes.title: Klipspringer

sections:
An easy trail through glorious fynbos with fabulous views  over Clarence Drive (R44). The start is
opposite the entrance to the Kogel Bay beach.
No permit is required.
(A fishing permit is required for a
ccess to the beach
.)
The trail starts with a steep, rocky 100m ascent  up to the plateau that runs along above the R44, but below the high ridge that is a key feature of the R44 drive. Once on the plateau, the path is easy, sandy and well maintained.  After running along the plateau for 3 km it descends back down to the R44.
There is a steep zigzag path that climbs 600m to the top of the ridge.  It meets a jeep track there that runs all the way from Steenbras Dam to Rockview Dam, but access along the jeep track is not permitted.  So this would only be 600m up to admire the view and 600m down. Strictly for the crazy fit!  Excluding that 'diversion' the trail is about 8km and could be walked in 2-3 hours, but this is a trail to be savoured, not rushed. Sit down, listen and watch the sunbirds perch on a nearby branch.
Start clearly marked.  Parking is a short way up the road to the left.
Well maintained, sandy paths with bridges over streams
After descending from the plateau, the path becomes 'interesting' as it crosses the wide boulder field created by the 2023 floods that destroyed many sections of the R44.  The path across is vague with few cairns (2026) but that could change after any flooding. If the path is not visible, simply go straight across.  There is a clear path out the other side, hidden until one steps on it.
Descent down loose boulders to cross the  boulder field
Looking upsteam
Looking downstream. Note the large concrete water tank hanging periously in mid-air.
The 'little' stream that one can step across.  Beware if flooding!
They must be joking!  This is immedietly after crossing the boulder field where no path is visible.  But a reassurance that one has arrived at the correct exit.
Taken from the bridge on the R44.  Amazing that the bridge survived the torrent of rocks that washed down.
From the bridge, looking towards Kogel Bay  beach. Walking back to the parking along the beach instead of the road would be nice, but access difficult. And it would be a very unpleasant walk along the loose boulders, so unless you are a purist and masochist,  stick to the road.

routes.title: Kogelberg Trail
routes.grade: 1****: Easy but long (~24km), with breathtaking natural beauty

sections.Location:
Kogelberg Nature Reserve
, off Clarence Drive (R44) between Betty's Bay & Kleinmond.
-
The route is marked
sections.Overview:
A long but easy walk circumnavigating Platberg (909m) through the wilderness of the Kogelberg Nature Reserve following the Palmiet, Louws & Oubos rivers. Cape Nature describes Kogelberg as their most beautiful reserve and this route certainly provides compelling evidence for this claim - you will struggle to find more beautiful fynbos & indigenous forests and the views of the Kogelberg Mountains and beyond are breathtaking. Permits can be bought at the gate for R65, there are a maximum of 26 sold per day.
There is very little shade in summer, however the Louws & Palmiet river are perennial and so water is not a concern. The oubos river has appreciable flow in autumn/winter.
sections.Route Description:
The route is well marked and in great condition, no written guide is necessary. It can be completed clockwise (Implied as the standard way by the trail markings) or anti-clockwise; the clockwise direction quickly completes 1/3 of the total elevation and brings upon the beautiful oubos forest very soon. The anti-clockwise is perhaps the better choice as it allows for more gradual elevation gain and conveniently places the forest as a convenient lunch spot.
Officially the route makes use of a jeep track running parallel to the Palmiet river, it is strongly recommended to take the much more interesting Palmiet River walk trail; this is a flat 1st class walk and adds one extra km to the walk (25km total).
The images are taken for the anti-clockwise direction using the Palmiet River Walk trail.
The Palmiet River
At the confluence of the Louws, Dwars & Palmiet Rivers. Dwarsrivier Peak on the left
The jeep track then heads west for 5.5 km
Louws River
Koelberg - the small dome infront. Sanctuary peak covered by clowd to the left.
Blousteenberg to the left with Sanctuary, Koelberg and the massive Kogelberg all onbstructed by the clowd cover. A band of indigenous forest seen on the left
Look carefully, you can see Swartkop & Simonsberg above Simon's Town.
On the side of Platberg overlooking Disa kloof which terminates at the Harold Porter Botanical Gardens.
Another patch of indigenous forest at the top of Disa Kloof
This section of the path is blooming with Ericas
Perdeberg seen in the distance
The first steps into the Oubos forest
A short but steep descent seperates the forest in two. The ecohuts & Cape Nature office in the distance
The path is very reminiscent of Skeleton Gorge
Platberg as seen from the descent between the two forest sections (March 2025 - Erosion has since occured)

routes.title: Betty's Bay to Hangklip via Sea Farm

sections.Location: Betty's Bay
sections.Overview:
An interesting and varied coastal walk starting from Pringle Bay, traversing over the Brodie's Link Reserve and down to the beach at Betty's Bay.
Then follows the coastline around the Sea Farm Private reserve to finish at Pringle Bay below the cliffs of Groot Hangklip.
Variation
: Do the walk one-way by doing a shuttle.
sections.Route Description:
See the slide show
An interesting variation which avoids the long walk along the road from Pringle, is to go up Hangklip from Pringle Bay, then down to Sea Farm and back via the Brodie Link.  See the OSM map for the paths.
sections.One way:
Meet at Baugarten Road, Betty's Bay, then shuttle to the boat launching ramp at the end of Hangklip Rd, Pringle Bay. The finish is then along Silversands Beach. Or walk the other way, depending on tides. It's best to walk Silversands at low tide - soft sand is tiring!

routes.title: Steenbras Ridge
routes.grade: 3 *** on the edge (2 if one moves to the right)

sections.Location:
On the north side of Steenbras Gorge, 6km south of Gordon's Bay. See also
Crystal Pools
and
Boskloof Ridge
. See
Crystal Pools
for access information and a parking map.
sections.Overview: An enjoyable cross-country scramble up to Steenbras Peak from where a variety of options area available, returning either straight down to the R44, or more interestingly, continuing along the ridge (known as the Dinosaurus-kam!) as far as one wants, then dropping down to the jeep track and returning via Crystal Pools. Good all year round given that it is a south facing climb and one can finish with a swim or two or three.
sections.Route Description:
Start on the Crystal pools path until shortly after the first river crossing.  Where the path rises to a low nek, turn off up the slope (no path) before the path drops back down to the river. Follow the ridge keeping as far to the left as possible for some grade 3 scrambling or keep further right (this is bushy) for easier grade 2 walking.
At the top,  go left to reach the top of Steenbras Peak. From here there are a range of options.  For a quick descent, drop straight down the gully on the other side of Steenbras to the R44 (1 hour).
More interesting is to continue traversing along the so called Dinosaurus-kam over peak 1B (next to Steenbras), Peak 2, Peak 3, Peak 4 and if you are really energetic Peak5. You do need to go either over or round Peak 2 and Peak 3 before traversing down and right to reach the jeep track that runs down from Steenbras Dam to the top of Crystal Pools.  Follow the jeep track and before it ends take the path that cuts off right across a stream and over a shallow nek to pick up the main Crystal Pools path.
Hermit's House
: A fascinating find just off the top of peak 1B was a well hidden and well constructed "cave house" complete with tables and chairs, a stove, kitchen, etc. It even had glass windows expertly fitted into the cracks and a camouflaged fiberglass door.  A date inscribed on the wall indicated that the hideout had been in use for 10 years or more.
Opening party
: 2 June 2008
Tony Heher
, Margie Growse, Kathleen Holtzhausen, Lucille Krige, Martyn Trainor, Elizabeth Trew (The route may have been done before but no cairns were found and asking around found no one who had any recollection of it being climbed.)
MM Steenbras Ridge

sections:

The
shows the  extensive network of trails in the area.
Eskom have provided 2 Hiking trails and a Mountain Bike circuit in the Koeberg reserve around the Nuclear Power station. They also have an Education centre which is excellent, but opening hours are limited.
All these facilities are a good advertisement for Eskom's 'green' attempts.
The short
Grysbok trail
starts next to the Info Centre so a combined visit is practical provided you are able to be there during the unfortunately limited opening times. The combination is ideal for youth groups, but a great pity is that the trail does not give access to the beach section.
The
Dikkop trail
has sadly been amended and now entails walking too much on some of the roads and most significantly no longer crosses the huge sand dunes which were one of the main attractions. Apparently Eskom management believed hikers were unable to follow the route markers across the sand fields. See also the
Dikkop Trail
page for more details.

shows the  extensive network of trails in the area.
Eskom have provided 2 Hiking trails and a Mountain Bike circuit in the Koeberg reserve around the Nuclear Power station. They also have an Education centre which is excellent, but opening hours are limited.
All these facilities are a good advertisement for Eskom's 'green' attempts.
The short
Grysbok trail
starts next to the Info Centre so a combined visit is practical provided you are able to be there during the unfortunately limited opening times. The combination is ideal for youth groups, but a great pity is that the trail does not give access to the beach section.
The
Dikkop trail
has sadly been amended and now entails walking too much on some of the roads and most significantly no longer crosses the huge sand dunes which were one of the main attractions. Apparently Eskom management believed hikers were unable to follow the route markers across the sand fields. See also the
Dikkop Trail
page for more details.

routes.title: Postberg Flower trail

sections:
Although situated in the West Coast National Park, this trail is on Private Land managed by SAN Parks, and it is only open to the public for the limited few months of the Flower season ie August ending 30th September.
The SAN Parks entrance fee is payable at the gate off the West Coast road, or free entry to Wild Card holders, then in addition an admission fee to the Postberg section is R50 pp as at September 2011, and it is advisable to phone book (022 772 2144) as the 1 and 2 day trails overlap and Hiker numbers per day are controlled.
The trails are very popular and it is advisable to book some months in advance, especially weekends.
Postberg

routes.title: Blackburn Buttress

sections:
The picture above and the dotted line Route shown is with acknowledgement to Southern Peninsula Classics (2019) by Tony Lourens. The route is graded B+ and takes 4 to 5 hours for the round trip. NB do not do this route in wet weather, and consider having a rope to protect the less experienced members of the party on the rock scrambling sections. The one serious difficulty is a small waterfall which could be very dangerous when wet. Currently the route is overgrown with vegetation and is best not attempted until some clearing has been done.
Full description of the route is published in Tony Louren's Guide "Southern Peninsula Classics'
Esme Beamish advised that she and a group intend doing some clearing when the weather improves later in 2025. Photos by
Eva Van Belle.

routes.title: Blackburn Major
routes.grade: 3 ** Easy cross-country scrambling (grade 2 most of the way)

sections.Overview: The route is across country with no path up the buttress but by keeping to the ridge, there is very little bush, so it is a pleasant clean route.  There is some minor scrambling on the way and one 6m grade 3 waterfall. The waterfall is generally dry but may be wet after heavy rain so avoid then. The route is relatively easy to find and is well marked with cairns.
sections.Route Description:
There are several ways to approach the route. One can either start at Silvermine (at the dam) and come half way down Blackburn Ravine, or up Blackburn ravine from East Fort, or along the contour path from Chapman's Peak. The route from Silvermine is described below. The others are obvious variations and don’t need describing.
From Silvermine Dam, go up the path towards Elephant’s Eye and then across to the lookout at the top of Blackburn Ravine. (If unsure how to get to Blackburn, consult a Silvermine map – Mountain Meanders generally does not describe the obvious paths that are described elsewhere!  Or see the maps and GPS tracks on the
Silvermine
page.)
There are two options for getting to the contour path: Either continue down Blackburn Ravine path to the junction with the contour path and then south towards Chapman's Peak.  This is the recommended route and is straight forward.  Although about 1 km longer it most probably takes about the same time because it is on a path all the way.
The opening party took a cross country line because we were looking for a possible high level traverse across to the buttress and also because the only clear, close up view of the buttress is from along this line.  This is described for completeness.   Come 140m (in elevation) down Blackburn Ravine. Finding the take off point from the Blackburn path is tricky. The Blackburn Ravine path zig zags down in several major and a few minor zig zags. Trying to count them is difficult. However, the far left zig only touches the vertical face of Blackburn Buttress at three points. There is a blind path leading off at the first zig-zag that touches the face. Ignore this – it only goes 20-30m to a lookout point. At the third place where the path touches the left hand face, take a faint path off left. At this point the path down to East Fort also swings far over to the right hand side of Blackburn.
The faint path rapidly fades out and one simply follows a cross country left diagonal descent. The line is not critical. If one descends too sharply one meets the East Fort to Chapmans path a bit sooner and if one traverses too much, one will end up above some rock bands. Simply move right to easier ground and continue the descent. From the take off in Blackburn Ravine to the contour path is only 350m but is quite rough going, dodging through clumps of proteas. This is why the descent down Blackburn Ravine to the junction with the contour path may be a better option - longer but quicker.
Once on the contour path, walk south towards Chapman’s Peak. Depending on where one got to the contour path it’s 200-300m along the contour path into the ravine that separates the two Blackburn buttresses (or about 1km if one came down Blackburn to the contour path). Cross the ravine (good water stop in the shade) and about 150m further on, when the ridge is visible, leave the contour path and head straight up. The difficulty with the route is that it is not possible to see the route ahead because of the intervening rockbands.  One needs to keep a 'picture' in one's head of the whole buttress to aid navigation. At the first rockband go slightly right to pass it up an easy ramp, then veer left to keep to the rocky ridge. One can keep straight on up but this takes one through bushy broken ground and is best avoided.
Near the bottom of gully three (which is visible at this stage), one comes up against a small buttress.  Go right and about 50m up a gully. It has one grade 3 move. As soon as possible move left onto a platform directly below an interesting 'cups and saucers' pitch.  And easy traverse to the left then takes one across a (horrible looking) steep grassy gully (no 2 in the picture) and then an ascending diagonal across a steepish grass slope takes one into the foot of the third gully. The dry waterfall in the gully looks difficult but by starting on the left and going up a set of steps leading diagonally right and then back left, it is easily climbed (grade 3 - or maybe only 2.5!).  A short scramble up this and one is on top, popping out unexpectedly in the middle of the Panorama path.
There are several options for the return. If starting from Silvermine Dam, the quickest is to turn right (south) when reaching the Panorama path and return to the dam either via Noordhoek Peak or direct. If the route has been approached from East Fort than it could be included in a longer day, returning over Noordhoek Peak and down to the contour path near the nek up to Chapman’s Peak, and from there back to East Fort. Or one could start on Chapman’s Peak road, go up to the contour path, along to Blackburn Buttress and down either via Noordhoek Peak or Blackburn Ravine i.e. many variations are possible. Pick what suits you!
Opening party
: 25 May 2010 Tony Heher (leader), Colin Bridge, Gael Culhame, Peggy deKock, Moiragh Girdwood, Margie Growse, Roger Hendry, Kathleen Holtzhausen, Lucille Krige, Anne Price, Martyn Trainor, Elizabeth Trew, Marge Vermark (as part of a U3A CMCA meet .)
Note
: No records have been found of this route having been done before, but any additional information is welcome. No cairns were found anywhere, and given that old climbers almost always placed cairns, it seems it is new.  The route is now well marked with cairns and should be easy to follow.
Blackburn Major

routes.title: Noordhoek Minor
routes.grade: 5 (or 3) **** The tricky rock step (5) can be bypassed (3)

sections.Overview:
A short fun route up the buttress with stupendous views over Hout Bay and Noordhoek. The best route has an exposed
grade 5
rock step that should be done with a rope (unless the party is very experienced), but there is an alternative grade 3 escape route. Being on the south side of the buttress, the route is cool and should be avoided in winter as it gets wet. The finish up the ridge is a very pleasant, but exposed, grade 4.
NB:  A rope is strongly advised on the exposed step up from the ledge.  An unroped  climber fell to his death on this route on 2 Feb 2017
sections.Alternate starts:
There are a number different ways to approach the route and it can be included in a variety of "mix-and-match" options e.g. from Chapman's Peak Drive, from East Fort and along the contour path, down Blackburn Ravine and along the contour path, etc.  This description is based on a start at Silvermine dam.
From Silvermine Dam, take the path up to Noordhoek Peak. Shortly before the peak, take the path that leads down towards Chapman’s Peak. Follow this down to 420m, about 500m before the junction with the Chapman’s to Blackburn contour path.  The path levels out across a small vlakte at this point. (There are some cairns just off the main path.)
Take off cross country (at map ref NH01) going down the left side of a small water course, cross the water course near the bottom and rejoin the contour path about 100m further on.  There are cairns all the way. Take the contour path north for 600m, passing the turnoff for Noordhoek West ridge route (NH02) after 300m (look carefully, it’s hard to spot.)
The turnoff from the contour path (NH03) is about 100m after crossing a water course that comes down from between Noordhoek Peak and Noordhoek Minor. It is up through the first obvious break in a small rock band after crossing the gully. Follow the ridge up to a small 3m rockband with several small caves along it. This is about 2 hours from the start and makes a good tea spot.
Continue left along the base of this band to an obvious break, and continue up to the next major rock band – about 300m up at the 560m level. Skirt this rockband to the left and find an obvious break through the band using a small chimney. Continue on up towards the main face of the buttress, bearing left and then up.
The buttress is marked by a prominent pinnacle at the end of the ridge.  The ledge and traverse that is being aimed for is higher up and not easily visible until one has climbed higher and up to the right skirting the base of the buttress. This is a decision point: either go left along the ledge, or skirt the buttress to the right until an obvious gully appears on the left which leads to the top. An even easier (but boring!) option is to continue straight on up the broad open gully to the Panorama path.
The ledge ends at a steep step that looks unclimbable from a distance, but in fact has some key footholds which makes it an easy Grade 5. The move up the rock step is however very exposed and the use of a rope is advised (See the note below for the tragic consequences of free climbing this section). Shortly after the step, go up diagonally
right
on good rock (instead of continuing straight) to avoid the loose gully and then traverse left to the nek.  This broken ground is easy (grade 3) but exposed and needs to be climbed with care as there is some loose rock.
From the nek, climb straight up the exposed, steep ridge on clean rock with good grips (grade 4). There is an alternative escape route off to the left at this point if anyone does not like the ridge.  The ridge eases off after 20-30m and continues on pleasant, easy scrambling to the summit. The final 5m onto the summit is a bit more of a challenge,  but worth doing. (There is an escape to the left.)  The summit is actually a small stand-alone pinnacle in front of the main ridge, so scramble down the other side and up to the main ridge where the Panorama path is met.
The obvious return route is south back down the Panorama path, but one could also go north along the Panorama path to Blackburn Ravine and return on the other side of the Silvermine valley. But there many other options especially if using one of the alternate starts.
Looking down into the buttress from Noordhoek Peak, showing the traverse out to the nek and the finish up the ridge as well as the escape route up the gully.
The ledge leading to the rock step – and from there up to the small nek (just out of picture
Opening party
: 17 Nov 2009, (left to right) Tony Heher, Liz Trew, Peggy de Kok, Kathy Holtshausen, Moiragh Girdwood, Lucille Krige, Barbara Clark & Martyn Trainor (not in pic). This is the "regular" U3A CMCA (Cape Mountains for the Curious and Adventurous) group.
The opening story
: on the 20 Oct 2009, a U3A CMCA meet explored up the ridge. Not having any ropes with us, we exited on the escape route instead. But intrigued by the possibilities, we returned a month later to complete it. No cairns were found and all indications are that this is a new route.
sections.Acknowledgments:
Thanks to Martyn Trainor for many of the pictures. It took four meets to get all the pictures that were needed! Thanks also to the intrepid CMCA band for joining the explorations.
2nd ascent: MCSA meet 22 Mar 2012
(From left to right) Richard Ferguson (who lead from the RD - so it does work!), Viv Marais, Thordis Sixt, Norman Cooper, Eric Harley, Rolf Spaeth, Moiragh Girdwood, Dennis Lange, Heleen Du Toit, Jeanne Myburgh and Tony Heher (not in pic).
sections.Comments:
A delightful old-style trad route with a beneficial dose of fitness maintenance ascent - very worthy of a repeat
What a stunning awesome daring astounding exciting beautiful best worlds view climb...   I enjoyed every second of it
I think I would find the way, after having done it once and using the RD, but I would not have felt comfortable without the security of the rope. The rest was a bit of a challenge, but good fun
Nordhoek Minor

routes.title: Noordhoek Peak Gully

sections:
Looking up the gully from a lookout on Chapmans Peak Drive. Noordhoek Minor on top left.
This gully route was opened by Hilton Davies and friends after a severe winter storm landslide caused a washaway that mostly cleared the gully during 2023.
The route pioneered was interesting, but awkward in places that required advanced rock climbing ability..

routes.title: Noordhoek NW Ridge
routes.grade: 5 one exposed pitch ***

sections.Location: Silvermine,  NW ridge of Nordhoek Peak
sections.Overview: A long bush wack and short scramble to the top of Noordhoek Peak
sections.Route Description:
Can be approached either from Chapmans Peak (adds 300m vertical) of from Silvermine (recommended).
Proceed up the Nordhoek path and then turn off down to Chapmans Peak. About half way down (500m contour), turn off across country on an ascending rights traverse through broken ground to the base of the main Nordhoek cliff face.  Not easy to find. Look for cairns or use the OSM MAp.
Zig-zag up for about 30m to a long, exposed traverse which ends in an open book. Climb this 10m grade 5 pitch. It is exposed so a rope is advised.
Continue scrambling on easy ground to the summit. Numerous return options.  Take your pick.
NOrdhoek NW Ridge

routes.title: Duiker Ridge

sections.Location:
Sandy Bay.
Overview
:  Follows a line all the way up the Western ridge of Karbonkelberg starting at the wreck of the Bos.
sections.Route Description:
From the Sandy Bay parking area at the top of Helgarde Estate, follow the 'Rocket Road' until above an old concrete bunker building. Follow a sandy path thickly overgrown with bush down to about 50m above the coastline. The path improves at this point. Continue South to the wreck of the Crane ship with a few rock steps along the way and lovely views of the coast.
A short way beyond ascend the ridge through some Pine trees (which could disappear eventually). The main difficulty of the route is a series of rock terraces on the right hand side of the ridge, which need careful balance as some moves are over a drop.
Above this there are more short scramble sections until the top of the ridge flattens out. Meander over and through some deep clefts to open terrain. Here you can ascend the steep and strenuous slope up to Karbonkelnerg. If one keeps to the left on the skyline, one emerges into the WW2 bunkers, or go up to the right and come out at a shallow neck. Both are quite bushy.
About 200m after passing through the old WW2 radar station buildings, descend to the saddle and up and over to SutherPeak to pick up the descent path back to the Sandy Bay parking.
Alternatively, continue on down the old jeep track to Hout Bay (needs cars at both ends.).
MM Duiker Ridge
